blocks.content: Every layer of the responsibility stack introduced in the previous topic has a security dimension too. AWS formalizes exactly where that security line sits with one specific, official framework, and understanding it precisely is not optional.
1. Shared Responsibility Model, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: 1. Shared Responsibility Model, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: The AWS Shared Responsibility Model is AWS's official framework describing exactly which security responsibilities belong to AWS and which belong to you, the customer, for any given AWS service you use.

AWS summarizes this framework with a single, memorable phrase: AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud, while you are responsible for security in the cloud, a distinction this topic examines in full, concrete depth.

This is not a vague, aspirational statement. It is a precise, documented framework that directly determines who is accountable when something goes wrong, and misunderstanding it is one of the most common sources of real world AWS security incidents.
Every security related topic covered throughout the rest of this course, particularly the entire Security Services module later on, assumes this framework as its foundational starting point.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736056957-136188596.png
blocks.alt: Shared responsibility model given its own full depth

blocks.content: 2. Security Of the Cloud Versus Security In the Cloud
blocks.text: 2. Security Of the Cloud Versus Security In the Cloud

blocks.content: Security of the cloud, AWS's responsibility, covers the physical data centers, the hardware, the network infrastructure connecting AWS's facilities, and the virtualization layer that isolates one customer's resources from another's.

Security in the cloud, your responsibility, covers everything you configure and control within that infrastructure: your data, your identity and access management configuration, your network security group rules, and, depending on service model, your operating system patching.

This split directly maps onto the IaaS, PaaS, SaaS spectrum from the previous topic: the more of the stack AWS manages on your behalf, the more of the security responsibility shifts to AWS as well, and the less remains yours to handle.

For an IaaS service like EC2, you retain responsibility for operating system patching and application level security. For a PaaS service like many managed database offerings, AWS handles more of that same responsibility automatically on your behalf.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736058574-240053196.png
blocks.alt: Security of the cloud, owned by AWS, versus security in the cloud, owned by the customer

blocks.content: 3. A Real Shared Responsibility Example

Consider an S3 bucket, AWS's object storage service, covered in full depth in Module 4. AWS is fully responsible for the physical security of the data centers storing that bucket's underlying data, and for the durability and availability of the S3 service itself.

You, the customer, are fully responsible for configuring that bucket's access permissions correctly, deciding who can read or write to it, and ensuring it is not accidentally left publicly accessible when it should genuinely be private.

A significant number of real world, publicly reported data breaches involving AWS have traced back not to any failure on AWS's side of this line, but to a customer's own misconfigured S3 bucket permissions, squarely within the customer's own responsibility.

This example is not hypothetical. It is one of the most commonly cited real world illustrations of the shared responsibility model in practice, and it directly motivates the S3 access control best practices covered in Module 4 later in this course.

# AWS secures the physical data center and the S3 service itself
# You are responsible for this bucket policy being correctly configured
aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket my-company-data

blocks.content: 4. Recap: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, Now Given a Security Dimension
blocks.text: 4. Recap: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, Now Given a Security Dimension

blocks.content: The previous topic established the stack of responsibility across four layers, application, runtime, operating system, and hardware, purely in terms of who manages each layer operationally, without yet addressing the security implications of that split.

This topic adds precisely that missing security dimension: whichever layer you manage operationally under the previous topic's framework is also, without exception, the layer you are responsible for securing under this topic's framework.

This connection is not a coincidence. It is the direct, logical consequence of the previous topic's stack: operational responsibility and security responsibility move together, both shifting toward AWS as you move from IaaS toward SaaS.

Understanding these two topics as one connected idea, operational responsibility and security responsibility tracking each other precisely, is the correct way to build genuine, lasting fluency with how AWS structures accountability.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736061709-274034395.png
blocks.alt: Recap of IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, already covered above, now given a security dimension

blocks.content: 5. What AWS Handles on Your Behalf
blocks.text: 5. What AWS Handles on Your Behalf

blocks.content: AWS's side of the shared responsibility line includes physical security of every data center, environmental controls such as power and cooling, the physical network infrastructure, and the hypervisor layer isolating customers from each other.

AWS also handles the security of its own managed services at whatever layer those services abstract away, meaning a fully managed service genuinely removes more security responsibility from you than a raw, unmanaged compute resource does.

This is precisely why choosing a more managed service, PaaS or SaaS over raw IaaS, covered as a deliberate choice in the previous topic, has a genuine security benefit as well as an operational one: less of the stack left for you to secure correctly yourself.

AWS invests enormous resources into this side of the responsibility line, resources that would be genuinely difficult and expensive for any individual customer organization to replicate independently, which is itself one of the concrete benefits covered in the Why Cloud topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736064207-706154058.png
blocks.alt: AWS's responsibility versus the customer's responsibility, split clearly

blocks.content: 6. What Remains Your Responsibility, Regardless of Service Model
blocks.text: 6. What Remains Your Responsibility, Regardless of Service Model

blocks.content: Certain responsibilities remain yours regardless of how far along the IaaS to SaaS spectrum a given service sits: your own data's classification and protection, your identity and access management configuration, and your own application level security decisions.

Identity and access management specifically, covered in complete depth in Module 2 immediately following this one, is arguably the single most consequential piece of your side of the shared responsibility line, since misconfigured permissions are a leading cause of real world security incidents.

Client side data encryption, network traffic protection for data you control, and correctly configuring any security related settings a given AWS service exposes to you all remain your responsibility no matter how managed the underlying service is.

This list is not exhaustive, but it captures the responsibilities that recur constantly throughout this course, particularly in the Security Services module, and understanding them now sets correct expectations for everything covered there later.
7. A Common Mistake: Assuming AWS Secures Everything
blocks.text: 7. A Common Mistake: Assuming AWS Secures Everything

blocks.content: A common and genuinely dangerous mistake is assuming that because AWS is a large, security focused company, it automatically secures every aspect of a customer's deployment, including configuration choices that are explicitly and unambiguously the customer's own responsibility.

This mistake directly caused the real world S3 breach pattern covered earlier in this topic: teams assumed AWS's general reputation for security meant their own specific bucket configuration was automatically safe, when bucket permissions were never AWS's responsibility to configure correctly.

The shared responsibility model is not a marketing reassurance. It is a precise, documented line, and treating anything on your own side of that line as automatically handled by AWS is a direct, avoidable path toward a real, serious security incident.

The fix is a deliberate habit: for every AWS service you use, explicitly identify which specific responsibilities fall on your own side of the line, and verify those specific items are genuinely, correctly configured, rather than assuming they are handled.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736065768-371577821.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of assuming AWS secures your own misconfigured S3 bucket for you

blocks.content: 8. The Shared Responsibility Model and Compliance
blocks.text: 8. The Shared Responsibility Model and Compliance

blocks.content: Compliance certifications, such as the ones referenced in the Public vs Private vs Hybrid Cloud topic earlier in this module, typically apply specifically to AWS's own side of the shared responsibility line, not automatically to your own configuration choices built on top of it.

This means an organization can be using AWS infrastructure that is itself fully compliant with a given regulatory framework while still being out of compliance overall, purely due to its own misconfigured settings on its own side of the responsibility line.

Genuine compliance requires attention to both sides of the line: confirming AWS's own certifications cover the specific framework required, and separately, deliberately configuring your own side correctly according to that same framework's requirements.

This distinction is a frequent source of confusion during real world compliance audits, where an organization mistakenly assumes AWS's certification alone satisfies the audit, without accounting for its own configuration responsibilities.
9. A Second Real Example: EC2 Security Groups
blocks.text: 9. A Second Real Example: EC2 Security Groups

blocks.content: Consider an EC2 instance, an IaaS resource covered in the previous topic. AWS is responsible for the physical security of the hardware running that instance and for the hypervisor isolating it from other customers' instances on the same physical machine.

You are responsible for that instance's security group configuration, the virtual firewall rules determining which network traffic can actually reach it, and for keeping its operating system patched against known vulnerabilities.

A misconfigured security group accidentally allowing broad, unrestricted inbound access is squarely a customer side responsibility failure, exactly analogous to the S3 bucket example covered earlier in this topic, but for network access rather than storage access.

This second example, alongside the S3 example, demonstrates that this pattern, a powerful service with a genuinely useful default posture undermined by a customer side misconfiguration, recurs across many different AWS services, not just one specific one.

# AWS secures the hypervisor and physical hardware
# You are responsible for this security group being correctly scoped
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0

blocks.content: 10. Documenting Your Own Responsibility Boundaries

A genuinely mature security practice involves maintaining explicit, written documentation of exactly which responsibilities fall on your own side of the shared responsibility line for every significant AWS service your organization actually uses in production.

This documentation becomes a concrete, actionable checklist during onboarding new team members, during security audits, and during incident response, replacing implicit, potentially inconsistent individual understanding with a single, shared, explicit source of truth.

Building this documentation incrementally, starting with the highest risk services such as S3 and IAM, covered in complete depth in the very next module, is a genuinely practical way to begin without needing to document every single service at once.

This habit connects directly to the Well-Architected Framework's Security pillar, covered later in this module, which explicitly calls for this kind of deliberate, documented security posture rather than relying on informal, undocumented understanding.
11. The Shared Responsibility Model Across Deployment Models
blocks.text: 11. The Shared Responsibility Model Across Deployment Models

blocks.content: The shared responsibility line shifts somewhat depending on the deployment model covered earlier in this module: private cloud generally shifts more responsibility onto you, since you own or exclusively control more of the underlying infrastructure yourself.

Public cloud, this course's primary focus, keeps the shared responsibility line exactly where covered throughout this topic, with AWS handling physical infrastructure and you handling your own data, access, and configuration choices built on top of it.

Hybrid architectures require tracking two distinct responsibility boundaries simultaneously, one for the public cloud portion and a genuinely different one for the private infrastructure portion, adding real complexity worth accounting for explicitly.

Recognizing this interaction between deployment model and shared responsibility reinforces why these two topics, covered earlier and here in this module, are best understood together rather than as entirely separate, unrelated concepts.
12. Applying This Model in Practice

For every new AWS service adopted, a genuinely useful habit is explicitly listing what falls on AWS's side of the responsibility line and what falls on your own, using the IaaS, PaaS, SaaS classification from the previous topic as a starting guide.

AWS's own documentation for each service typically states its specific shared responsibility boundaries explicitly, and consulting that documentation directly, rather than assuming based on general intuition, is the most reliable way to get this right.

Building this habit early, before it is needed during an actual security review or incident, means the team already has a clear, documented understanding of its own responsibilities well before any problem actually surfaces.

This habit connects directly to Module 7, Security Services, and Module 2, Identity and Access Management, both of which assume this shared responsibility understanding as an already established foundation.

13. Best Practices for the Shared Responsibility Model
blocks.text: 13. Best Practices for the Shared Responsibility Model

blocks.content: Explicitly identify your side of the responsibility line for every AWS service adopted, rather than assuming based on AWS's general reputation for security, exactly as covered in this topic's common mistake section.

Consult AWS's own service specific documentation for shared responsibility details, since the exact boundary can differ meaningfully between services even within the same broad IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS category.

Prioritize identity and access management configuration specifically, given how consistently it appears as a leading cause of real world incidents squarely within the customer's own side of the responsibility line.

Revisit your own responsibilities whenever adopting a new AWS service or migrating an existing workload to a more or less managed service tier, since the responsibility boundary shifts along with that service model change.

blocks.content: 14. The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

The Shared Responsibility Model is AWS's precise, documented answer to who is accountable for what: AWS secures the cloud itself, and you secure what you put into and configure within it, with no ambiguity once you understand where the line sits.

Assuming AWS automatically handles something on your own side of that line, exactly the mistake behind countless real world S3 breaches, is one of the most avoidable, most consequential security mistakes an AWS engineer can make.

The next topic, AWS Global Infrastructure, shifts focus away from security responsibility and toward the physical, worldwide footprint of data centers that everything covered in this module ultimately runs on top of.

Keep the security of the cloud versus security in the cloud phrase firmly in mind. It is short enough to remember under pressure, and precise enough to correctly resolve nearly any real world question about whose responsibility a given security concern actually is.
This topic is now fully covered; AWS Global Infrastructure, making that physical side of the line concrete, follows immediately next.
Every security related module later in this course, particularly Module 2 and Module 7, assumes this precise division as its starting foundation.
AWS secures of, you secure in. Never assume otherwise.

blocks.title: Shared Responsibility Model In Full
points: The Shared Responsibility Model precisely divides security accountability: AWS secures the cloud itself, physical infrastructure and virtualization, while you secure what you configure and put into it.
This division tracks the IaaS, PaaS, SaaS spectrum from the previous topic directly: the more AWS manages operationally, the more it also secures on your behalf.
Identity and access management, data classification, and service configuration remain your responsibility regardless of how managed a given service is.
Assuming AWS automatically secures something on your own side of the line is a common, genuinely dangerous mistake, responsible for real world incidents like misconfigured S3 buckets.
AWS Global Infrastructure, covered next, shifts focus to the physical, worldwide footprint of data centers everything in this course ultimately runs on top of.
